#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
When kubelet detects that it's under resource pressure, it first attempts to do soft evictions, until the hard eviction threshold is reached. When a pod is soft-evicted, it respects the configured max pod grace period seconds, and until the pod has shut down, kubelet will not attempt to soft OR hard evict another pod, even if the hard eviction threshold is reached.

As a result, one pod taking a long time to shut down can cause kubelet to run out of resources. From [this comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/016d8b11ae250ca933fe83de312bbe7c4945cd20/pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager.go#L405) and [this comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/016d8b11ae250ca933fe83de312bbe7c4945cd20/pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager.go#L603) this behavior seems to be by design

In our case, we saw one soft eviction take 7 hours to complete, and meanwhile, resources usage kept climbing without any automation trying to save the node. Had other pods gotten soft evicted while this pod shut down, this would not be an issue. Manual intervention prevented it from reaching hard-eviction thresholds, but had that not happened, this would have entirely exhausted the node with no automated action.

This fixes that by:
1. No longer waiting on soft evictions to complete. There is a semaphore to prevent concurrent soft evictions, but the eviction loop will resume after one soft eviction starts, so as to catch when we reach the hard eviction threshold
1. If we reach the hard eviction threshold, evict the pod that is the worst offender- this is can be a pod that has been previously soft evicted but is taking a while to shut down

This also changes the ordering of thresholds. Previously, it was ordering thresholds by prioritizing memory first, and thresholds with no resource to reclaim last, and now it also considers whether or not the threshold is a hard threshold. This is needed so that when something has resource pressure, it will first consider the hard threshold - because we want to immediately hard evict once we've reached that point.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:

Hey @olyazavr! Thanks for your contribution!

I've noticed that the eviction manager waits for pods to be cleaned up before calling `synchronize()` again:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/79c61d5f0305c566b642be978b1e4837870db257/pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager.go#L201-L214

My concern is that your changes would never take effect, as `synchronize()` would be called only when the original pods set for eviction are already gone.

I think that you did not catch this in your unit test since you call `synchronize()` directly.

Also, see [my comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/123872#issuecomment-2029612383) on the issue for general thoughts.

/cc

> Why would eviction takes 7 hours? It seems the grace period for a soft eviction is set this high.

Our infrastructure runs a mix of workloads. Many of our pods can be evicted quickly, while others may have an extended prestop hook running.

We generally  allow for pods to have 24h+ termination grace periods to accommodate workloads that are really inconvenient to kill. For example, a database pod running a migration may take a very long time to complete, and killing it prematurely would potentially result in losing days of progress. Meanwhile, the node could have 100 other pods running on it that are all able to be evicted very quickly and prevent the node from hitting a critical disk threshold. So the problem we see is that kubelet can get stuck evicting a pod with really slow termination, when there are plenty of other pods that are low-hanging fruit.

@iholder101 Yes that's true, but it only waits for the pod to be cleaned up for [up to 30s](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/79c61d5f0305c566b642be978b1e4837870db257/pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager.go#L432), so in my case it would time out and then continue the loop again (I tested this on our own cluster)

This was discussed in the sig node weekly meeting, and the desired outcome is that if a pod that is taking too long to soft-evict, and we have breached the hard-eviction threshold, it should be hard evicted. This is currently not possible until https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/113883 is merged (this allows for grace period to be shortened). As for the rest of this PR (eg. trying to evict others if we're still in the soft-evict stage), I was told it would be reviewed later

Could I get some clarity on what needs to be done here? 
Some options I see:
1. wait for 5m (configurable) after soft-eviction and then re-run through the eviction loop again, possibly evict (hard or soft) another pod
1. wait for 5m (configurable) after soft-eviction and then re-run through the eviction loop again, only taking action if we have exceeded the hard eviction threshold and we need to hard evict a different pod (but keep track of when the first soft-eviction completes, sort of like a soft-eviction semaphore)
1. wait for 5m (configurable) after soft-eviction and then re-run through the eviction loop again, only taking action if we have exceeded the hard eviction threshold and if the original pod we soft-evicted isn't done yet, hard-evict it (this can only happen once https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/113883 is merged)

> Could I get some clarity on what needs to be done here? Some options I see:
> 
> 1. wait for 5m (configurable) after soft-eviction and then re-run through the eviction loop again, possibly evict (hard or soft) another pod
> 2. wait for 5m (configurable) after soft-eviction and then re-run through the eviction loop again, only taking action if we have exceeded the hard eviction threshold and we need to hard evict a different pod (but keep track of when the first soft-eviction completes, sort of like a soft-eviction semaphore)
> 3. wait for 5m (configurable) after soft-eviction and then re-run through the eviction loop again, only taking action if we have exceeded the hard eviction threshold and if the original pod we soft-evicted isn't done yet, hard-evict it (this can only happen once [The second time the pod is deleted the grace period does not take effect #113883](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/113883) is merged)

I think about the changes in this PR as two unrelated changes:
1. **Fixing the bug**: currently a pod with a large grace period can block hard evictions. This is a bug that definitely should be fixed.
2. **Changing behavior ("move to others" strategy)**: which needs to be discussed, and raises some concerns.

W.r.t. (2), I share @kannon92's [cocern](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/124081#discussion_r1551877028). A malicious/malfunctioning pod that allocates more and more memory over time and has a huge grace period will cause all of the pods on the node to be killed. @olyazavr [said](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/124081#discussion_r1551943189):

> Without this change, doing that would probably still kill all pods once resources are exhausted

This is true however just because of the bug (1) of blocking hard evictions. Conceptually the concern is still valid and true, even if the bug is fixed.

----

What I fail to understand at this point is why `evictPod()`/`killPod()` are blocking. I would vote for your second suggestion (number 2), but with a slight modification to remove the 5m wait:
* When soft-eviction threshold is met, evict a pod respecting its grace period WITHOUT BLOCKING.
  * Mark that the pod is being evicted, evict in the background, move on.
* Continue the eviction controller loop as usual.
  * If the pod is still evicting and the hard-eviction threshold is not met, avoid evicting more pods until the pod finishes evicting.
  * If a hard-threshold is met, re-evict the same pod without respecting its grace period.

This approach has the following advantages IMO:
1. Solves the bug explained above.
2. When a hard-eviction threshold is met, kubelet would react very quickly (and would avoid blocking the controller for 5 minutes).
3. A single malfunctioning/malicious pod cannot cause kubelet to kill all pods on the node.

WDYT?

> TBH I'm not entirely sure that's desired. Perhaps memory is so essential that we always want to address it first?

The memory ordering is still preserved. The only difference is that on top of the existing ordering, it will also then prefer thresholds with a hard eviction grace period (0). I can add more testing here

This is necessary because as I found out when running [the test](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/124081/files#diff-58409d75456e0bb4551c14340dc87d7960eccc733e7b6b68818b419cab6d395aR2877) I wrote- it's nondeteministic otherwise.

Say you have a threshold A for having 1Gi memory left with grace period 5m, and then threshold B for having 500Mi memory left with grace period 0. We start out having 1Gi memory left, so threshold A would be triggered, and a pod would be soft-evicted. Then, if the pod is taking a while to evict and meanwhile we're down to < 500Mi memory, it'll sometimes select threshold A (and not do anything since it is a soft threshold and we already have a pod evicting) OR it'll select threshold B (the desired outcome- it will hard evict that pod)
/retest

issue_context.title: Soft eviction of pods with long grace periods blocks hard evictions when under resource pressure
issue_context.body:
### What happened?

When kubelet detects that it's under resource pressure, it first attempts to do soft evictions, until the hard eviction threshold is reached. When a pod is soft-evicted, it respects the configured max pod grace period seconds, and until the pod has shut down, kubelet will not attempt to soft OR hard evict another pod, even if the hard eviction threshold is reached.

As a result, one pod taking a long time to shut down can cause kubelet to run out of resources. From [this comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/016d8b11ae250ca933fe83de312bbe7c4945cd20/pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager.go#L405) and [this comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/016d8b11ae250ca933fe83de312bbe7c4945cd20/pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager.go#L603) this behavior seems to be by design

In our case, we saw one soft eviction take 7 hours to complete, and meanwhile, resources usage kept climbing without any automation trying to save the node. Had other pods gotten soft evicted while this pod shut down, this would not be an issue. Manual intervention prevented it from reaching hard-eviction thresholds, but had that not happened, this would have entirely exhausted the node with no automated action

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect that kubelet would keep trying to soft evict other pods if one is taking a long time to shut down. Or at the very least, start hard evicting pods if the hard eviction threshold is reached. It could also hard-evict the pod that was soft-evicted but is taking a long time to shut down.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create two pods that get scheduled to the same node that have emptyDir volumes and a prestop hook that just sleeps forever
1. Start filling up those emptyDir volumes with `dd` until soft eviction threshold is reached
1. Watch as kubelet soft-evicts one pod
1. Continue filling up the emptyDir volumes with `dd`
1. Kubelet will not evict (hard or soft) even as the resource is totally exhausted

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

@olyazavr Could you add more details on the runtime (crio, containerd) and version information?

In general - I think that the use-case you're describing is valid - letting a pod take its time shutting down unless there's an emergency.

Another thought that I have is that if the majority of the pods on a pressured node are configured with a high grace period it might compromise the node that wouldn't be able to evict, stuck waiting for the pods to shut down (and AFAIK there is no admin-level way to control pods' grace-period without using a webhook).

> kubelet will not attempt to soft OR hard evict another pod, even if the hard eviction threshold is reached.

At a first glance this sounds strange to me.
Does it make sense to force-evict pods if the hard eviction threshold is reached?

> seems like something that would be fixed by grace period preemption in the kubelet cc @mrunalp @smarterclayton

Care to explain what you mean by this?

@iholder101 right now there's already a soft and hard eviction threshold, so if the hard eviction threshold is reached, it will evict pods with a grace period overridden to 1 (granted we need https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/124063 for that to work) : https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/79c61d5f0305c566b642be978b1e4837870db257/pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager.go#L408-L409
So this protects the node even if the grace period for soft evictions is set to a large value
